country.name: Israel
country.tagline: Bronze Age palace cellars, Rothschild's colonies and a modern industry that took winemaking up the Golan and into the desert.

stats.note: Approximate: about 5,000 to 5,500 ha of wine grapes and some 300 wineries; production around 40 million bottles. Not reported separately by OIV 2025.

country.overview:
Wine in the land of Israel is ancient, biblical and, after a long gap, very new. The Canaanite palace at Tel Kabri in western Galilee held a wine cellar of about 1700 BC with some 40 large jars and roughly 2,000 litres of wine flavoured with resins, honey and herbs: the oldest and largest palatial wine cellar known in the Near East. The Bible is full of vineyards and presses; Byzantine Gaza and Ashkelon exported wine across the Mediterranean, and in the Negev the Nabataean and Byzantine towns of Avdat and Shivta had large wine presses.

Islamic rule from the seventh century ended commercial wine for a millennium, though local grapes survived in Arab vineyards as table grapes and raisins. The modern industry was founded by Baron Edmond de Rothschild, owner of Château Lafite, who in the 1880s funded Jewish agricultural colonies and built wineries at Rishon LeZion (1890) and Zichron Ya'akov (1892), the origin of Carmel. For a century the industry made mostly sweet sacramental kosher wine.

The turn came in the late 1970s and 1980s, when University of California, Davis researchers identified the Golan Heights as a cool, high site, and the Golan Heights Winery (founded 1983, Yarden label) proved it with modern Cabernet, Chardonnay and sparkling wine. Domaine du Castel in the Judean Hills, Margalit, Yatir in the Negev, Clos de Gat, Recanati, Tzora and Flam followed, and the country now has about 300 wineries. The regions run from the Upper Galilee and the Golan (vineyards up to about 1,200 metres) through the Judean Hills and the Shomron to the Negev desert, where drip irrigation and high plateaus make viticulture possible.

Two features make Israel distinctive. Almost all large wineries are kosher, which involves rules on who handles the wine (Sabbath-observant Jews from crushing onward, unless the wine is heat-treated, mevushal), on fining agents and on agricultural laws such as orlah (no fruit from vines under four years) and shmita (the sabbatical year). And a research programme led by Ariel University and others has identified and revived ancient local grapes, among them Marawi (also called Hamdani), Jandali and Dabouki, as well as the red Bittuni, with Recanati and Cremisan bottling them.

Some of Israel's best-known vineyards lie in territory whose status is disputed. The Golan Heights were captured from Syria in 1967 and annexed by Israel in 1981, an annexation not recognised by the UN or most states (the United States recognised it in 2019); Israeli wineries in the West Bank are in territory considered occupied under international law. The EU requires that products from these areas not be labelled simply 'Made in Israel'.

history.title: The palace cellar at Tel Kabri
history.text: In 2013 excavators uncovered a storeroom in the Canaanite palace with about 40 large jars, around 2,000 litres in total, holding residues of a resinated, flavoured red wine.

history.title: Wine of Gaza and the Negev
history.text: Byzantine wine from Gaza and the Negev towns of Shivta and Avdat, which had large stone presses, was exported in 'Gaza jars' across the Mediterranean.

history.title: Mikveh Israel
history.text: The first Jewish agricultural school was founded near Jaffa and taught viticulture.

history.title: Rothschild's wineries
history.text: Baron Edmond de Rothschild funded the colonies of Rishon LeZion and Zichron Ya'akov and built their wineries (1890 and 1892), the core of Carmel.

history.title: The Golan Heights Winery
history.text: Founded at Katzrin after UC Davis advice identified the high Golan as a cool site; its Yarden wines started Israel's quality era.

history.title: Ancient grapes revived
history.text: DNA research identified local varieties such as Marawi (Hamdani), Jandali, Dabouki and Bittuni; Recanati bottled a Marawi from the 2014 vintage.

country.classification: Israel has an official list of wine regions (Galil with the Golan, Upper and Lower Galilee subregions; Shomron; Shimshon; the Judean Hills; and the Negev) used on labels, but no appellation system with yield or grape rules. Kosher certification (and mevushal status) is the most visible label distinction.
country.climate_soils: Mediterranean, with rainy winters and dry summers; every vineyard needs drip irrigation in summer. Quality depends on altitude: the Golan's basalt and volcanic tuff at 400 to 1,200 metres, Upper Galilee's limestone and terra rossa, the Judean Hills' limestone at 500 to 900 metres, and loess and sand in the Negev at up to 800 metres.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Petite Sirah, Carignan
grapes.note: The main reds; old-vine Carignan and Petite Sirah are local specialities.

grapes.name: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Gewürztraminer
grapes.note: Main whites; Chardonnay for traditional-method sparkling on the Golan.

grapes.name: Marawi (Hamdani), Jandali, Dabouki
grapes.note: Ancient local whites revived from Arab vineyards.

grapes.name: Argaman
grapes.note: An Israeli cross (Carignan by Souzão) bred for colour.

further_reading: Rogov's Guide to Israeli Wines, Daniel Rogov

sources.title: Wine Route of Israel / Israel Wine Producers Association

regions.name: Galilee and Golan Heights
regions.tagline: The coolest, highest vineyards: basalt on the Golan, limestone in the Upper Galilee.
regions.summary: Israel's quality heartland. The Golan Heights rise from the Sea of Galilee towards Mount Hermon, with vineyards up to about 1,200 metres on volcanic basalt and tuff; the Upper Galilee around Dalton and Kerem Ben Zimra and the Lower Galilee around Mount Tabor add limestone and terra rossa. The Golan is internationally regarded as Syrian territory occupied by Israel since 1967; Israel annexed it in 1981, an act recognised by the United States since 2019 but not by the UN.
regions.history: Golan Heights Winery (1983), Galil Mountain, Dalton, Recanati and Tabor built the region's reputation.
regions.terroir: Cooler nights, winter snow on the high Golan, volcanic and limestone soils.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Marawi.
regions.classification: Official wine region name Galil (subregions Upper Galilee, Lower Galilee, Golan Heights).

sources.title: Wine Route of Israel / Israel Wine Producers Association

regions.name: Judean Hills
regions.tagline: Terraced limestone around Jerusalem and Domaine du Castel.
regions.summary: Hills west and south of Jerusalem at 500 to 900 metres, on limestone terraces of biblical age, with wineries such as Domaine du Castel, Flam, Tzora, Clos de Gat and Sphera. Part of the area extends into the occupied West Bank.
regions.history: Ancient presses dot the terraces; Castel (1988) started the boutique wave.
regions.terroir: Limestone and terra rossa, cool nights.

sources.title: Wine Route of Israel / Israel Wine Producers Association

regions.name: Shomron
regions.tagline: Carmel's historic heartland around Zichron Ya'akov and Binyamina.
regions.summary: The official Shomron wine region covers the coastal hills south of Mount Carmel around Zichron Ya'akov and Binyamina, where Rothschild's Carmel winery stands, and the plain of Sharon.
regions.history: Rothschild built the Zichron Ya'akov winery in 1892.
regions.terroir: Coastal hills, limestone and marine sediments, warm.

sources.title: Wine Route of Israel / Israel Wine Producers Association

regions.name: Shimshon
regions.tagline: Between the coast and the Judean Hills, where Rishon LeZion's winery began.
regions.summary: Low hills and plains between the coastal strip and the Judean foothills, historically a large-volume area; Barkan, Carmel's Rishon LeZion and Teperberg draw on it.

sources.title: Wine Route of Israel / Israel Wine Producers Association

regions.name: Negev
regions.tagline: Desert vineyards on ancient Nabataean terraces.
regions.summary: Drip irrigation and high plateaus (Ramat HaNegev at about 800 metres, and the Yatir forest near Arad) make viticulture possible in the desert, echoing the Byzantine wine towns of Shivta and Avdat. Yatir Winery and around 50 small Negev wineries work here.
regions.history: Byzantine wine presses at Shivta and Avdat.
regions.terroir: Loess and sand, extreme diurnal swings, salt-tolerant management.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Petit Verdot, Chardonnay.

sources.title: Wine Route of Israel / Israel Wine Producers Association

sites.name: Tel Kabri palace wine cellar
sites.text: The Canaanite palace on the grounds of Kibbutz Kabri, near Nahariya, where in 2013 archaeologists found a storeroom of about 40 large jars, around 2,000 litres, with residues of red wine flavoured with resins, honey and herbs, dated to about 1700 BC. The palace also had Minoan-style frescoes and was destroyed by an earthquake.

sites.name: Carmel Winery, Zichron Ya'akov
sites.text: The cellars Baron Edmond de Rothschild built in 1892 for the colony of Zichron Ya'akov on Mount Carmel's southern slopes, still Carmel's winery and visitor centre.

sites.name: Carmel Winery, Rishon LeZion
sites.text: Rothschild's first great winery, completed in 1890 at Rishon LeZion, with historic underground cellars; long the heart of Israel's sacramental wine trade.

sites.name: Golan Heights Winery
sites.text: Founded in 1983 at Katzrin by Golan settlements, the winery behind the Yarden, Gamla and Golan labels and the first to prove the high Golan's potential for Cabernet and sparkling wine. The Golan is Syrian territory occupied by Israel since 1967.

sites.name: Domaine du Castel
sites.text: Eli Ben Zaken's family estate in the Judean Hills, founded in 1988 at Ramat Raziel, with its winery now at Yad HaShmona; its Grand Vin was among the first Israeli wines praised internationally.

sites.name: Shivta Byzantine wine presses
sites.text: A Byzantine town in the Negev (UNESCO Incense Route) with large wine presses and evidence that it made and exported wine in the sixth and seventh centuries.

sites.name: Avdat
sites.text: Nabataean and Byzantine city on the Incense Route in the Negev, with ancient wine presses on its hillsides.

sites.name: Dalton Winery
sites.text: In the Dalton industrial park of the Upper Galilee, part of a cluster of seven wineries including Recanati and Adir.

sites.name: Flam Winery
sites.text: The Flam family's winery in the Judean Hills near Eshtaol, one of Israel's leading boutique producers.

sites.name: Tabor Winery
sites.text: Winery at Kfar Tavor beneath Mount Tabor in the Lower Galilee, on chalk and terra rossa.
